source.title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals
source.authors: Xiaohan Qin; Xiangdong Zhang; Tuo Dai; Sunan Zou; Huaijin Wu; Yebin Yang; Zhuo Xia; Lin Yao; Yuliang Liu; Junchi Yan

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study runs a compute-scaling comparison and fits loss-versus-compute curves, but for training loss and residual-architecture variants rather than testing the specified held-out-loss laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The scaling experiment reports fitted training-loss curves across four model scales, iso-loss compute speedups, and loss reductions at the largest scale; these are recorded below. The downstream benchmark comparisons and 10B ablation losses do not test whether downstream performance is predictable with scale or whether the specified held-out scaling laws hold, so they are not recorded as rows. No cited results are treated as study results.
record.test_reason: The study fits a shifted power law (E fixed at 0.72) as a tool to compare residual architectures (Vanilla, mHC, AttnRes, MSAR). It reports only iso-loss speedups and relative loss reductions of its own method against baselines. It gives no fit quality, exponents, extrapolation check, held-out-loss law, or allocation analysis, so its results do not bear on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that MSAR improves the loss–compute trade-off (1.58× iso-loss speedup versus 1.35× AttnRes and 1.30× mHC) and downstream scores at 18B and 28B. They also suggest that multi-state and cross-layer residual benefits are complementary.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares residual architectures using matched backbones and training-token budgets across four scales, and fits a shifted power law to final training loss versus normalized compute. It does not reproduce the original studies' held-out-loss scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies by residual architecture (Vanilla, mHC, AttnRes, MSAR) and is evaluated at four model scales. The fit fixes E = 0.72 and uses ordinary least squares in log space; fit sensitivity is not tested.

fits_no_version.finding: Across four MoE scales (2.21B–17.40B), residual architectures shift the fitted loss–compute curve, giving iso-loss compute speedups of 1.30× (mHC), 1.35× (AttnRes) and 1.58× (MSAR) over Vanilla.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual-connection design changes the compute efficiency (offset of the loss–compute power law) of MoE language models.

fits_no_version.finding: At the largest scale, training-loss reductions versus Vanilla are 1.6% (mHC), 1.8% (AttnRes) and 2.7% (MSAR).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual architecture choice gives small but consistent final-loss reductions at fixed compute.

record.problems: The scaling-law experiment uses four model scales and reports no uncertainty estimates. Individual loss points and fitted exponents are not stated in the text and are available only in Figure 3; the fit fixes the irreducible loss at 0.72.
record.rows_left_out: No reported scaling-law results were left out. Downstream benchmark scores and 10B ablation results were excluded because they do not test the claim versions' specified scaling, extrapolation, allocation, architecture-shape, modality, or downstream-predictability relationships.

untested.parts: Training loss only, fitted over four points with fixed E. No goodness of fit, exponents, or held-out loss are reported.
Depth and width at fixed parameter count are not varied. Residual-connection type is not shape.
Downstream scores are compared across architectures, not predicted from scale or loss.
There is a single fitting procedure with no sensitivity analysis.

record.verdict_notes: Corrected the relation from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. The scaling-law fit is a measurement tool for an architecture comparison. Training loss, four points and a fixed irreducible loss with no reported exponents or fit quality mean the paper cannot test V1, V2 or V7. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The experiment measures final training loss, not held-out pretraining loss; it does not separately test parameter-count or token-count power laws.
No forecast fitted on smaller runs is evaluated against a larger run.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token allocation is performed.
The study compares residual architectures, not depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count as specified.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer settings are tested.
Downstream benchmarks are compared across residual variants, but downstream performance is not tested for predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
The paper uses one stated fitting procedure and fixed irreducible-loss estimate; it does not test sensitivity to fitting choices or whether curves bend away from a power law.
